title: Strict henselization as finite local lifts over the henselization
statement: Let $(A,\mathfrak m,\kappa)$ be a commutative local ring with residue field $\kappa$ [def-weil-residue-field]. Let $H=A^{\mathrm h}$ be its henselization, the universal local henselian extension of $A=A_{\mathfrak m}$ [def-weil-pbc-henselization-at-prime], with residue field identified with $\kappa$, and choose a separable closure $\kappa^{\mathrm{sep}}$ [def-pd-separable-closure]. For every finite separable subextension $\kappa\subset e\subset\kappa^{\mathrm{sep}}$, there is a finite local etale $H$-algebra $B_e$ (finite as an $H$-module and etale in the sense of [def-weil-etale-morphism]), unique up to unique isomorphism respecting an identification $B_e/\mathfrak m_HB_e\simeq e$. Every inclusion $e\subset f$ lifts uniquely to a local $H$-algebra map $B_e\to B_f$ inducing that inclusion on residues. These maps form a filtered diagram. Its colimit $C=\varinjlim_e B_e$ [def-weil-pbc-category-colimit] is a local ring with residue field $\kappa^{\mathrm{sep}}$, and there is a canonical $A$-algebra isomorphism, respecting the residue identification, from $C$ to the strict henselization of $A$ at this residue closure, defined by the pointed etale neighbourhood colimit [def-weil-pbc-strict-henselization-limit] of $\operatorname{Spec}A$, equivalently by the pointed-algebra colimit [def-sc-ring-strict-henselization]. Equivalently this is the strict henselization of $H$ at the same residue closure. Restricting the diagram to finite Galois subextensions $e/\kappa$ gives the same colimit (Galois means separable and normal: all minimal polynomials of elements split in $e$).

source.place: Tag 0BSL (remark-construct-sh-from-h), entire remark; finite Galois indexing is the cofinal subsystem obtained by taking the normal closure of a finite separable residue subextension.

proof.text: Put $K=\kappa^{\mathrm{sep}}$. For a finite separable subfield $e/\kappa$ of $K$, apply the finite separable field-lifting theorem over the henselian local ring $H$ to obtain a module-finite etale $H$-algebra $B_e$ with $B_e/\mathfrak m_HB_e\simeq e$. Every maximal ideal of $B_e$ contains $\mathfrak m_HB_e$ by the finite-algebra radical lemma. Since the quotient is the nonzero field $e$, its zero ideal is the only maximal ideal, so $B_e$ is local with maximal ideal $\mathfrak n_e=\mathfrak m_HB_e$. Its inverse image in $H$ is $\mathfrak m_H$, so the structure map is local. This proves locality rather than assuming that an arbitrary finite etale algebra is local.

source.place: Tag 0BSL (remark-construct-sh-from-h), first sentence; Tag 04GK (lemma-henselian-cat-finite-etale), essential surjectivity

proof.text: Reduction on homomorphisms between finite etale $H$-algebras is bijective. Lift each residue inclusion $e\subset f$ to its unique $H$-algebra map $u_{ef}:B_e\to B_f$. For $b\in B_e$, its residue maps to zero in $f$ exactly when its residue in $e$ is zero; hence $u_{ef}^{-1}(\mathfrak n_f)=\mathfrak n_e$, so the lift is local. The composite $u_{fg}u_{ef}$ and $u_{eg}$ have the same residue map, as do $u_{ee}$ and the identity; injectivity of reduction gives the diagram laws. For two lifts of the same identified field $e$, lift the identity in both directions; their composites are identities by the same argument. This gives precisely uniqueness up to unique residue-compatible isomorphism. The finite separable subfields of $K$ form a small directed poset containing $\kappa$, as in the filtered-colimit description of a separable closure. Thus this is a filtered diagram.

source.place: Tag 0BSL, arrows sentence, using Tag 04GK full faithfulness

proof.text: The small diagram has a colimit $C$ in commutative $H$-algebras, which is also its colimit in commutative rings; every element of $C$ comes from some $B_e$. The residue maps $B_e\to e\subset K$ give $\psi:C\to K$. This map is surjective because every element of $K$ belongs to some $e$ and $B_e\to e$ is surjective. If $c$ is represented by $b\in B_e$, injectivity of $e\to K$ shows that $\psi(c)=0$ exactly when $b\in\mathfrak n_e$. Consequently $I=\ker\psi$ is the union of the images of the $\mathfrak n_e$. If $c\notin I$, its representative $b$ is outside the maximal ideal of the local ring $B_e$, hence is a unit, and its inverse maps to an inverse of $c$. Since $C/I=K$ is nonzero, $I$ is the unique maximal ideal. Thus $C$ is local with the specified residue identification, and each $B_e\to C$ is local.

source.place: Tag 0BSL, union and residue sentences; Tag 04GI (lemma-colimit-henselian), omitted locality/residue argument expanded

proof.text: Each $B_e$ is henselian by the finite-local-algebra permanence theorem applied to $H\to B_e$. Hence $(B_e,\mathfrak n_e)$ is a henselian pair. Step 2 shows that the transitions carry these ideals into one another, and Step 3 identifies their image union with $I=\mathfrak m_C$. Apply preservation of henselian pairs under directed colimits to obtain that $(C,\mathfrak m_C)$ is henselian. Since $C/\mathfrak m_C=K$ is separably closed, $C$ is strictly henselian. No Noetherian or completeness assumption is used.

source.place: Tag 0BSL, henselianity sentences, using Tags 04GH (lemma-finite-over-henselian), 04GI (lemma-colimit-henselian); pair formulation: more-algebra.tex Tag 0FWT (lemma-filtered-colimits-henselian)

proof.text: As a filtered colimit of the etale $H$-algebras $B_e$, $C$ is ind-etale over $H$. The henselization ind-etaleness theorem applied to the maximal ideal of the local ring $A$ gives that $A\to H$ is ind-etale (identifying $A_{\mathfrak m}$ with $A$). Stability under composition therefore makes $A\to C$ ind-etale too. In particular both $H\to C$ and $A\to C$ have the filtered-etale presentations required by the henselian mapping lemma; their being filtered colimits is not being inferred from a universal-property definition of henselization alone.

source.place: Tag 0BSL, last two sentences, using Tag 04GN (lemma-henselization) and Tag 0BSI (lemma-composition-colimit-etale)

proof.text: Let $D_A$ be the colimit of etale residue triples over $(A,\mathfrak m,K)$. The strict-henselization triples theorem gives that $D_A$ is henselian local, ind-etale over $A$, and has its canonical residue map onto $K$; the triples-colimit identification makes it a strict henselization in the pointed-algebra sense. Apply the henselian mapping lemma first with source $C$, target $D_A$, and then with source $D_A$, target $C$, over the base $A$, prescribing the identity of $K$ on residue fields in both cases. Its hypotheses hold by Steps 3--5 and the triples theorem, and both maximal ideals lie over $\mathfrak m$. The resulting local maps have composites with residue identity. Uniqueness in that same mapping lemma, compared with each identity map, proves that both composites are identities. Thus $C\simeq D_A$ canonically as an $A$-algebra respecting the chosen residue identification.

Apply the same comparison over the local base $H$, with its identified residue field $\kappa$, to the strict-henselization triple colimit $D_H$. Steps 3--5 make $C$ henselian local, ind-etale over $H$, with residue field $K$; the triples theorem gives these properties for $D_H$. The two maps provided by the henselian mapping lemma with residue identity are inverse by its uniqueness, giving $C\simeq D_H$ as an $H$-algebra. The comparison in Step 6 respects the canonical $H$-structure on $D_A$: the composite $H\to C\to D_A$ is local and extends $A\to D_A$, so the universal property defining $H$ identifies it with the canonical map $H\to D_A$. This also explains compatibility of the two descriptions.

source.place: Tag 0BSL, construction from the henselization and uniqueness; Tags 08HR, 04GW

proof.text: To compare with geometric neighbourhoods even for imperfect $\kappa$, choose an algebraic closure $\Omega$ of $K$ and the geometric point $\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\to\operatorname{Spec}A$ through $A\to\kappa\to K$. The relative separable closure of $\kappa$ in $\Omega$ is exactly the given $K$: one inclusion follows from separable algebraicity of $K/\kappa$; if $x\in\Omega$ is separable over $\kappa$, its minimal polynomial over $K$ divides a separable polynomial over $\kappa$, so $K(x)/K$ is finite separable and therefore trivial because $K$ is separably closed. For every etale neighbourhood with residue embedding into $\Omega$, the etale-residue-field theorem says this residue field is finite separable over $\kappa$. Every element of its image is therefore in $K$. This verifies, rather than assumes, the image-containment hypothesis of the chart/triple equivalence used next.

source.place: Tags 04HT (remark-etale-neighbourhoods), 04HX (lemma-describe-etale-local-ring), residue-closure choice and proof first paragraph

proof.text: Use the affine-chart/triple equivalence with $Y=U=\operatorname{Spec}A$ and the geometric point of Step 8. Every affine neighbourhood already factors through $U$, and Step 8 verifies the required residue-image condition. The equivalence identifies the opposite affine pointed-neighbourhood category with the residue-triple category and identifies their ring diagrams, including the structural and residue maps. A cocone on either diagram gives a cocone on the other by this equivalence; their universal factorization properties are identical. Thus their colimits are canonically isomorphic, with the same maps from $A$ and to $K$. Taking a small representative category as in the neighbourhood-colimit definition does not change that universal property. Hence the ring $D_A$ of Step 6 is the strict henselization ring of the pointed scheme-neighbourhood definition, and Step 6 gives the claimed comparison with $C$.

source.place: Tag 04HX (lemma-describe-etale-local-ring), proof first paragraph and displayed triple colimit

proof.text: The separable-closure Galois theorem shows that $K/\kappa$ is Galois. Choose a finite $\kappa$-basis of any finite separable subfield $e$; the finite-set-in-finite-Galois-subextension theorem supplies a finite Galois subfield $g\subset K$ containing that basis, hence containing $e$. It also supplies a common finite Galois overfield for two such $g$'s, by applying it to the union of their finite bases. To see directly that restriction gives the same colimit, extend any cocone on the Galois subdiagram by sending $B_e$ to its target through $B_e\to B_g$ for a chosen $g\supset e$. A common Galois overfield shows independence of this choice and compatibility for every $e\subset f$. Extension and restriction are inverse on cocones and their maps. Their universal properties therefore give the same colimit, canonically and respecting both the $H$-structure and the residue maps.
